newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds end weaker amid dollar's decline.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds end weaker amid dollar's decline.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed weaker on Friday, hurt by a further decline in the Canadian dollar and weakness in the price of U.S. treasuries, analysts said.

"People have been really focused keenly on the dollar today. It certainly looks like the comments that were made, at least the ones we heard about in the press from the Bank of Canada, were not all that well received," said Rich Wylie, a fixed-income economist with TD Securities Inc.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond fell C$0.15 to C$106.80 to yield 7.407 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond fell 21/32 to yield 7.17 percent. The spread between the two narrowed to 24 basis points from 28 basis points at Thursday's close.

Both Canadian and U.S. bonds began the session lower after the release of U.S. retail sales and producer price reports for March. The retail sales report included upward revisions to January and February retail sales, while the PPI report showed the core PPI rate was stronger than expected.
The data helped fuel speculation that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike rates again in May. That, in turn, weighed on the Canadian dollar.

"Expectations that you're probably going to see higher interest rates from the Fed over the next couple of months, combined with the weaker dollar, has given our bond market reason for some selling today," said Wylie.
Canada's dollar weakened to as low as C$1.3988 (US$0.7149) this afternoon as investors sold off the currency for a second session, prompting the Bank of Canada to buy dollars on curency market.
The weakness in the dollar was linked to comments from Bank of Canada officials on Thursday suggesting the central bank was in no hurry to match the recent U.S. rate hike.
In other prices, the Government of Canada's 10-year benchmark bond fell C$0.10 to C$100.65 to yield 6.905 percent while the U.S. bond fell 13/32 to yield 6.97 percent.
The negative spread between the bonds widened to seven basis points from three basis points at the close of trading on Thursday.
The three-month cash T-bill yielded 3.22 percent against its U.S. equivalent which yielded 5.30 percent.
